question: In August 1947 British India was partitioned into independent India and Pakistan. The boundary line was drawn by a British barrister, Cyril Radcliffe, who had never visited India. Around 12-15 million people moved. Perhaps a million died in communal violence. What is the event called?
context: Lord Mountbatten was the last Viceroy. Kashmir's status was disputed from the start; three wars between India and Pakistan have followed.

question: In 1206 a kurultai of Mongol tribes acclaimed a new Great Khan. By 1227 he and his sons had conquered an empire stretching from China to the Caspian. Who was he?
context: His empire continued to grow under his sons and grandsons; at its peak it was the largest contiguous land empire in history.

question: From 1370 to 1405 a Central Asian conqueror who claimed Mongol descent built an empire based at Samarkand, killing perhaps 17 million in his campaigns. He left pyramids of skulls in conquered cities and was lamed by an early wound. By what name is he known?
context: He died at 68 marching on China. His tomb at the Gur-e Amir in Samarkand still stands.

question: Around 1325 a wandering people called the Mexica settled on an island in the marshy Lake Texcoco in central Mexico, where their priests had seen an eagle on a cactus eating a snake. They built a city that became one of the largest in the world. What was it called?
context: When Cortes arrived in 1519 the city had around 200,000 inhabitants — larger than any city in Europe at the time.

question: Around 1450, the Inca emperor Pachacuti built a stone royal estate on a saddle 8,000 feet up in the Andes between two peaks. The Spanish never found it. Hiram Bingham brought it to Western attention in 1911. What site?
context: The site survived intact because the conquistadors never knew of it. The Incas had no wheel, no writing, and no iron — yet built precision stonework still standing.

question: Between roughly 1100 and 1450, a Shona kingdom in southern Africa built massive dry-stone walls — the largest sub-Saharan stone structures south of the pyramids. The country named for the ruin became independent in 1980. What is the site called?
context: The site had been mistakenly attributed by colonial archaeologists to Phoenicians or Arabs. Twentieth-century work confirmed it as a Shona achievement.

question: Around AD 330, the Aksumite king Ezana of what is now Ethiopia adopted Christianity, making his kingdom one of the earliest Christian states in the world. What other Christian state had converted earlier?
context: Aksum's stelae — tall granite obelisks — still stand. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church traces an unbroken line to the 4th century.

question: On 1 March 1896, at a battle in the highlands of northern Ethiopia, the Emperor Menelik II crushed an invading Italian army of 17,500, killing or capturing most of them. What did the victory secure?
answer: Ethiopian independence in the age of European colonisation of Africa
choices: Ethiopian independence in the age of European colonisation of Africa
Italian withdrawal from Eritrea by the end of the year
British protection of Ethiopia as a buffer state
Ethiopian conquest of much of the Horn of Africa
context: Ethiopia remained the only African state never colonised by Europeans, except for Italian occupation 1935-41 under Mussolini.

question: On 11 February 1990, after 27 years in South African prisons including 18 on Robben Island, a 71-year-old anti-apartheid leader walked out a free man. Who was he?
context: He had been jailed since 1962. He shared the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize with President F. W. de Klerk and was elected president in 1994.

question: Around 1235 a prince from a small Malinke kingdom in West Africa defeated the king of Sosso at the Battle of Kirina and founded an empire that lasted three centuries. His exploits are still sung by griots. Who was he?
context: The Epic of Sundiata is West Africa's national epic, comparable to the Iliad or the Odyssey.

question: In May 1832, the French mathematician Evariste Galois, age 20, spent his last night writing furiously and scrawling 'I have not time' in the margins. He was shot in a duel at dawn and died of his wounds. What field did the margins essentially found?
answer: Group theory — the algebraic study of symmetry
choices: Group theory — the algebraic study of symmetry
Non-Euclidean geometry — alternatives to Euclid's postulate
Real analysis — the rigorous study of continuous functions
Number theory — the study of integers and prime distributions
context: Galois's letters to his friend Auguste Chevalier explained the theory; Liouville published them in 1846 and the field eventually became foundational to modern algebra.

question: On 7 June 1954, Alan Turing — the British mathematician who had broken the German Enigma code at Bletchley Park and helped invent the modern computer — was found dead in his bed in Wilmslow at 41. He had been chemically castrated by court order two years earlier. What was beside him?
answer: A half-eaten apple, presumed laced with cyanide
choices: A half-eaten apple, presumed laced with cyanide
A loaded pistol still warm in his hand
A note in his own writing addressed to his mother
An unfinished proof of the Riemann hypothesis
context: The 1952 conviction had been for 'gross indecency' over a homosexual relationship. The UK government apologised in 2009 and Queen Elizabeth granted a posthumous pardon in 2013.

question: In early 1913 a 25-year-old self-taught Indian clerk in the Madras Port Trust wrote to the Cambridge mathematician G. H. Hardy with strange theorems and identities. Hardy at first thought it a hoax. Who was the writer?
context: Ramanujan came to Cambridge in 1914. He died of tuberculosis in 1920 at 32, leaving notebooks that mathematicians have continued to mine to this day.

question: Working in a converted shed in Paris in the late 1890s, a Polish-born physicist named Marie Curie and her husband Pierre processed tons of pitchblende to isolate two new radioactive elements. One they named for her homeland, one for the rays they emitted. Name the second.
context: She won Nobel Prizes in physics (1903) and chemistry (1911) and was the first woman to win in both disciplines. Her notebooks are still radioactive.

question: On 8 May 1794, during the French Reign of Terror, the chemist who had named oxygen, written the first modern chemistry textbook, and shown that combustion was a reaction with that element was led to the guillotine for his past work as a tax farmer. Who was he?
context: Judge Coffinhal reportedly said 'the Republic has no need of savants'. The mathematician Lagrange said: 'It took them but an instant to cut off that head, and a hundred years may not produce another like it.'

question: In a single year — 1905 — a 26-year-old patent clerk in Bern, Switzerland published four papers that overturned physics. One explained Brownian motion; one the photoelectric effect; one introduced special relativity; one gave us E=mc^2. Who was he?
context: He won the Nobel Prize in 1921 — for the photoelectric effect, not for relativity. His general theory of relativity came in 1915 and was confirmed by the 1919 solar eclipse.

question: In 1909, in a Manchester laboratory, a New Zealand-born physicist had his students fire alpha particles at thin gold foil. Most went through; a few bounced almost straight back. He said it was like firing 15-inch shells at tissue paper and having them come back. Who was he?
context: The experiment showed that atoms have a tiny dense nucleus and are mostly empty space. Rutherford had already won the Nobel Prize in chemistry for radioactivity work.

question: On 24 November 1859 a book by an English country gentleman, who had sat on his theory for 20 years, went on sale in London. It sold out on its first day and reshaped biology. Who was the author?
context: Wallace had independently arrived at the same theory; the papers were jointly read in 1858. The 1860 Oxford debate between Huxley and Bishop Wilberforce became legendary.

question: In May 1881, at a farm at Pouilly-le-Fort south of Paris, the French chemist Louis Pasteur set up a public demonstration: 25 sheep vaccinated against anthrax versus 25 unvaccinated. He returned in June. What had happened?
answer: All 25 vaccinated sheep survived; nearly all unvaccinated sheep had died
choices: All 25 vaccinated sheep survived; nearly all unvaccinated sheep had died
All sheep had survived; the bacterial sample had been weakened too far
All sheep had died; the trial was a public embarrassment
Most unvaccinated sheep had survived; the trial was inconclusive
context: The demonstration turned germ theory into a working tool. Pasteur went on to develop the first human rabies vaccine in 1885.

question: On 17 December 1903, on a windy beach in North Carolina, two Ohio brothers achieved the first powered, controlled, sustained, heavier-than-air human flight. Their longest flight that day lasted 59 seconds and covered how far?
context: Five witnesses from the local lifesaving station saw the flight. They had built the plane in a Dayton bicycle shop.

question: On 20 July 1969, around six hours after the lunar module Eagle landed in the Sea of Tranquillity, a 38-year-old former Navy test pilot stepped onto the Moon's surface. Who was he?
context: His statement was 'that's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind'. He may have intended 'one small step for a man'; transmission cut the article.

question: From 3 to 9 August 1936, at the Olympic Games staged by Adolf Hitler as Aryan propaganda, an Alabama-born son of sharecroppers won four gold medals: 100m, 200m, long jump, and 4x100m relay. Who was he?
context: He set or equalled three Olympic records and a world record. He and German long-jumper Luz Long became friends; Hitler refused to shake his hand.

question: On 6 May 1954, on a windy cinder track at Iffley Road in Oxford, a 25-year-old British medical student broke a barrier many had thought physically impossible. Who was he?
context: His time was 3:59.4. Australian John Landy broke his record six weeks later. Bannister went on to a distinguished career in neurology.

question: On 30 October 1974, in Kinshasa, Zaire, a 32-year-old Muhammad Ali, regarded as past his prime, used a strategy he later called 'rope-a-dope' to absorb George Foreman's punches and knock him out in the eighth round. What was the fight called?
context: Ali had been stripped of his title in 1967 for refusing the Vietnam draft. The Rumble brought him back to the top of the sport.

question: On 22 February 1980, at Lake Placid, New York, a US Olympic hockey team of amateurs and college players defeated the Soviet team — winners of the past four Olympic golds and arguably the greatest hockey team ever assembled. The score?
context: Coach Herb Brooks had told his team: 'You were born to be a player. You were meant to be here. This moment is yours.' The US went on to beat Finland for gold.

question: On 29 March 1987, before a record indoor crowd of around 93,000 at the Pontiac Silverdome in Michigan, Hulk Hogan body-slammed Andre the Giant — billed at 520 pounds — and pinned him to retain the WWF title. What was the event called?
context: It is widely considered the moment professional wrestling became American mainstream entertainment. Bob Uecker and Aretha Franklin appeared on the card.

question: In April 1997, a 21-year-old playing in his first Masters as a professional won by 12 strokes — the largest margin in Masters history. He shot 270, breaking the tournament record. Who was he?
context: He became the first golfer of African American or Asian descent to win the tournament. Lee Elder, the first black man to play the Masters in 1975, came to watch.

question: On 14 June 1998, in Game 6 of the NBA Finals against the Utah Jazz, with 5.2 seconds left and the Chicago Bulls down by one, Michael Jordan hit a jumper from the top of the key to win the series. What did he do to Bryon Russell first?
answer: Pushed off — a contact the referees did not call
choices: Pushed off — a contact the referees did not call
Faked left to clear the lane completely
Drew a foul that put him at the line
context: It was Jordan's sixth title in eight years and his last game as a Chicago Bull. He retired (for the second time) that summer.

question: On 31 October 1517, by tradition, the Augustinian monk Martin Luther nailed a Latin list of 95 disputation points to the door of the castle church at Wittenberg in Saxony. The list attacked one specific Catholic practice. Which?
choices: The use of Latin in worship
context: Within months printed copies were circulating across Germany. The Reformation that followed ended Western Christian unity for 500 years.

question: On the evening of 24 May 1738, an Anglican priest reluctantly went to a small religious meeting on Aldersgate Street in London. He heard a reading of Luther's preface to Romans. Something happened that he described in a single famous phrase. Who?
context: Wesley went on to found the Methodist movement and to preach perhaps 40,000 sermons in a long life of constant travel.

question: On 12 September 1962, before a crowd of 40,000 at Rice University Stadium in Houston, President John F. Kennedy made the case for the Apollo programme. He used a memorable line about choosing a hard goal. What did he say?
answer: We choose to go to the Moon, not because it is easy, but because it is hard
choices: We choose to go to the Moon, not because it is easy, but because it is hard
We must reach for the stars before our enemies do
Our gaze is fixed on heaven; our feet are on the Earth
If freedom is to survive, it must lift off the ground
context: He did not live to see it. Apollo 11 landed on 20 July 1969, eight years after his speech and six years after his assassination.

question: On 26 June 1963, before a crowd of around 450,000 in the city square then called Rudolph Wilde Platz in West Berlin, John F. Kennedy gave a speech that ended with four German words declaring solidarity with the people of the divided city. What four words?
context: The speech is widely regarded as one of the most powerful of the Cold War. The square was renamed John F. Kennedy Platz that November after his death.

question: On 4 June 1940, after the evacuation of Dunkirk and as France collapsed, the British Prime Minister told the House of Commons that Britain would fight on the beaches, in the fields, in the streets, and in the hills. How did the speech end?
choices: We shall fight on the seas and oceans
We shall defend our island, whatever the cost may be
Whatever the cost in blood and sweat
context: Churchill spoke from his cabinet papers. The phrase 'we shall never surrender' has come to define British resolve in 1940.

question: On 8 December 1941, the day after the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, the President of the United States addressed a joint session of Congress in just over six minutes. He opened with one famous phrase. What was it?
answer: A date which will live in infamy
choices: A date which will live in infamy
The day our patience ran dry
context: Congress declared war on Japan that afternoon by 388 to 1. The lone dissent came from Jeannette Rankin, the first woman elected to Congress.

question: On 4 March 1933, at his first inauguration as President of the United States, Franklin D. Roosevelt tried to rally a country in the depths of the Depression with a sentence about fear. How did he put it?
answer: The only thing we have to fear is fear itself
choices: The only thing we have to fear is fear itself
A coward dies a thousand times; the brave only once
No one can make you feel inferior without your consent
We must wage war on want and fear
context: He went on to launch the New Deal in his first hundred days. He served as President until his death in April 1945, longer than anyone before or since.

question: On 19 November 1863, at the dedication of a soldiers' cemetery on the battlefield where Union troops had turned back Robert E. Lee that summer, Abraham Lincoln spoke for about two minutes. How does the speech end?
answer: Government of the people, by the people, for the people
choices: Government of the people, by the people, for the people
With malice toward none, with charity for all
Now we are engaged in a great civil war
A house divided against itself cannot stand
context: Edward Everett spoke for two hours before Lincoln. Everett wrote to Lincoln: 'I should be glad if I could flatter myself that I came as near to the central idea of the occasion in two hours as you did in two minutes.'

question: From 12 March to 6 April 1930, a slight man of 60 in homespun cotton walked 240 miles from Sabarmati to the Indian coast at Dandi, where he picked up a handful of salt in defiance of a British monopoly. Who?
context: By April, around 60,000 Indians had been arrested for breaking the salt law. Gandhi was imprisoned in May. India became independent 17 years later.

question: On 5 June 1989, the morning after the People's Liberation Army cleared Tiananmen Square, a lone man in a white shirt stood in the middle of Chang'an Avenue in front of a column of tanks. He blocked them, climbed up, spoke to the driver, then was pulled away by onlookers. What is he called?
context: His identity has never been confirmed. Jeff Widener of the Associated Press took the most famous photo from the Beijing Hotel. Several other photographers got the shot.

question: On the evening of 9 February 1964, an estimated 73 million Americans — around two-fifths of the country — watched four young men from Liverpool perform on a Sunday night variety show in New York. Who were they?
context: Crime in the US reportedly dropped during the broadcast. The Beatles played 'All My Loving', 'Till There Was You', and 'She Loves You' in the first set.

question: In late April 1937, German and Italian aircraft of Franco's nationalist coalition bombed a Basque town on a market day in support of the Spanish Civil War. Pablo Picasso painted a vast black-and-white canvas of the horror for the 1937 Paris World's Fair. What town?
context: The painting stayed in the Museum of Modern Art in New York until Picasso's wish — that it return only to a democratic Spain — was honoured in 1981, eight years after his death.

question: On 7 May 1824, the premiere in Vienna of Ludwig van Beethoven's Ninth Symphony — the first symphony of the standard repertoire to use voices — climaxed with a setting of Schiller's poem. What was the choral section called?
choices: Song of the Earth (Mahler's later work)
Hymn to the Stars (an imagined sequel)
context: Beethoven was so deaf he had to be turned around by a singer to see the audience applauding. He died less than three years later.

question: On Christmas Eve 1968, the three astronauts of Apollo 8 — the first humans to orbit the Moon — closed a live television broadcast back to Earth by reading aloud from a sacred text. Which?
answer: The opening verses of the Book of Genesis
choices: The opening verses of the Book of Genesis
The Sermon on the Mount from Matthew
Psalm 23 — the Lord is my shepherd
The opening verses of the Gospel of John
context: Frank Borman, James Lovell, and William Anders took turns. Anders had also taken the Earthrise photograph the day before. They circled the Moon ten times.

question: On 14 February 1990, at the request of Carl Sagan, NASA turned the Voyager 1 spacecraft around — 6 billion km from home — and took a photograph of Earth as a tiny point of light. What did Sagan call the image?
context: His reflections on the photograph — that 'every saint and sinner in the history of our species lived there' — became one of the great popular meditations of the late 20th century.

question: In March 415 a Christian mob in Alexandria attacked one of the last great scholars of the ancient world — a Neoplatonist philosopher and mathematician who had taught Greek philosophy and astronomy. She was dragged from her chariot and killed. Who was she?
context: She had been advisor to Orestes, the Roman prefect of Egypt. The Patriarch Cyril of Alexandria — later canonised — was widely blamed at the time.

question: Around 431 BC the Athenian general Thucydides began a meticulous history of the war between Athens and Sparta, refusing myth and seeking causes. He was exiled in 424 BC after a failed command. What is his book called?
answer: The History of the Peloponnesian War
choices: The History of the Peloponnesian War
The Histories of the Greek World
context: Thucydides is the founder of scientific history. The work breaks off mid-sentence in 411 BC; its account of the Melian Dialogue is a touchstone of realist thought.

question: Around 387 BC, after the execution of his teacher Socrates, the Athenian philosopher Plato founded a school in a sacred grove outside Athens dedicated to a local hero. The school operated for nearly nine centuries. What was it called?
context: Aristotle joined as a student at age 17 and stayed twenty years. The Academy was closed by Justinian in 529 AD as the last pagan school.

question: Around 335 BC, after tutoring the young Alexander of Macedon, the philosopher Aristotle returned to Athens and founded a school outside the city gates. Students walked with him as he taught. What was the school called?
context: His followers were called Peripatetics, from the walking. Aristotle's surviving lecture notes shaped Western thought for two thousand years.

question: In the 4th century BC the Cynic philosopher Diogenes of Sinope lived in a large clay jar in the marketplace of Athens. One famous story has him walking the streets in daylight carrying a lit lamp. What was he searching for?
answer: A single honest man in the city of Athens
choices: A single honest man in the city of Athens
A pupil worthy of his teaching
The shortest path to the agora
A silver coin he had lost at dawn
context: Diogenes mocked convention and reportedly told Alexander the Great to stand out of his sunlight. He claimed the title 'citizen of the world.'

question: Around 440 BC the Greek writer Herodotus of Halicarnassus published a long prose work investigating the causes of the Greco-Persian Wars and gathering customs from across the known world. Cicero later gave him a title. What is it?
context: He travelled to Egypt, Mesopotamia, and Scythia and recorded what he heard. Thucydides corrected him into a more critical method a generation later.

question: On the island of Cos in the late 5th century BC, the Greek physician Hippocrates broke with priestly healing and taught that disease has natural causes. What oath, attributed to his school, is still echoed by physicians?
answer: An oath to do no harm and to keep professional secrets
choices: An oath to do no harm and to keep professional secrets
An oath of poverty in service to the gods of healing
An oath to share all discoveries with the public assembly
An oath of obedience to the magistrates of the city
context: The Hippocratic corpus is a collection of texts from his school; the famous oath dates to roughly the same period.

question: Around 600 BC, on the Greek island of Lesbos, a poet composed personal lyric verse on love, longing, and women's lives. Plato later called her the tenth muse. Who was she?
context: Only fragments of her nine books survive, mostly in papyri found at Oxyrhynchus in Egypt. The English adjective 'sapphic' derives from her name.

question: Around 594 BC the Athenian poet and statesman Solon was given emergency powers to reform a city torn by debt slavery and aristocratic dominance. He cancelled debts and gave the poor a vote in the assembly. What is his reform called?
answer: The Seisachtheia, or 'shaking off of burdens'
choices: The Seisachtheia, or 'shaking off of burdens'
The Lycurgan constitution, modeled on Sparta
The Cleisthenic tribes, by district rather than clan
The Periclean franchise, paying citizens for jury service
context: After his reforms Solon left Athens for ten years so the laws would not be undone. Aristotle ranked him a founder of Athenian democracy.

question: Around 438 BC the Athenian sculptor Phidias completed a colossal statue, nearly 12 meters tall, of the city's patron goddess for her new temple on the Acropolis. It was made of ivory and gold over a wooden frame. Which goddess?
context: Phidias also made the gold-and-ivory Zeus at Olympia, one of the Seven Wonders. Both statues are lost; we know them from coins and ancient descriptions.

question: Around 307 BC the philosopher Epicurus bought a garden outside Athens and gathered friends, including slaves and women, to live and study there. He taught that pleasure, defined as freedom from pain and fear, was the highest good. What was his school called?
choices: The Academy, or Grove of Hecademus
context: Lucretius would later versify Epicurean physics in De Rerum Natura. The Christian Fathers attacked Epicurus; 'epicure' as glutton is a slander on his actual teaching.

question: Around 300 BC the philosopher Zeno of Citium began teaching under the Painted Porch at the north edge of the Athenian agora. He held that virtue alone is the good and external things are indifferent. What was his school named for?
answer: The Stoa, or porch, where he taught
choices: The Stoa, or porch, where he taught
The Lyceum, or wolf-shrine, where he walked
The Cynosarges, or white-dog-altar, where he prayed
The Academy, or grove, where he had studied
context: Stoicism shaped Cicero, Seneca, Epictetus, and Marcus Aurelius. The school flourished for five centuries.

question: In 458 BC, with a Roman army surrounded by the Aequi, the Senate sent envoys to a farmer plowing his small field across the Tiber and named him dictator. He raised an army, won the war in 15 days, resigned the office, and returned to the plow. Who was he?
context: He became a Roman ideal of civic virtue. Washington was likened to him; the city of Cincinnati and the Society of the Cincinnati bear his name.

question: In 44-43 BC the Roman senator Cicero delivered a series of fierce speeches against Mark Antony's bid for power, naming them after Demosthenes' attacks on Philip of Macedon. Antony had him hunted down and killed. What were the speeches called?
context: Cicero's severed head and right hand were nailed to the Rostra in the Forum. His writings became the model of Latin prose for two thousand years.

question: Around 29 BC the poet Virgil began an epic in twelve books, modelled on Homer, telling how a Trojan refugee named Aeneas founded the line that would become Rome. Dying in 19 BC, Virgil asked that the unfinished work be burned. What did Augustus do?
answer: Overruled the request and had the poem published
choices: Overruled the request and had the poem published
Honored the request and the work was lost
Had it completed by another poet, Ovid
Had the manuscript sealed in his own tomb
context: The Aeneid became the foundational poem of Latin literature. Augustus is glorified in its prophecies of Rome's destiny.

question: Between AD 101 and 106 the emperor Trajan conducted two wars beyond the Danube against the kingdom of Dacia. The campaigns are sculpted in spiral relief on a 30-meter marble column still standing in Rome. What did the conquest provide?
answer: Vast Dacian gold that funded public works and a famous festival
choices: Vast Dacian gold that funded public works and a famous festival
A peace treaty that paid annual tribute to Rome
A buffer client kingdom that never paid Rome again
A failed campaign that cost Trajan his throne
context: Trajan extended the Empire to its greatest size. Dacia is the ancestor of modern Romania, whose language remains Latin-derived.

question: Between AD 122 and 128 the emperor Hadrian had a stone barrier built across northern Britain, 117 km long, with milecastles and forts. It marked the northern limit of the Roman Empire. What was its purpose?
answer: To control movement and guard against raids from northern tribes
choices: To control movement and guard against raids from northern tribes
To channel the river Tyne for irrigation of Roman farms
To house the legionaries' wives and children in security
To mark the religious boundary of the cult of Mithras
context: Long stretches still stand. Hadrian travelled the empire personally; he also rebuilt the Pantheon in Rome.

question: In 73 BC a Thracian gladiator broke out of a training school in the southern Italian city of Capua with around 70 fellow gladiators using kitchen knives and skewers. The escape grew into a slave revolt that lasted two years. Who led it?
context: At its height the slave army numbered around 100,000. Pompey, returning from Spain, claimed credit for crushing the last remnants after Crassus had broken Spartacus's main force.

question: In October AD 732, near the city of Tours in central Gaul, a Frankish army on foot under a chief called 'the Hammer' stopped a Muslim raiding force advancing from Spain. Who was the Frankish leader?
context: The defeat checked Muslim expansion north of the Pyrenees. Pepin would depose the last Merovingian; Charlemagne would rebuild the empire.

question: Around 1209 a young man from a wealthy cloth-merchant family in the Umbrian town of Assisi gave away his inheritance, wore a rough tunic, and began preaching poverty and care for lepers. The order he founded received papal approval that year. Who was he?
context: He is the patron saint of animals and ecology. Tradition says he received the stigmata on Mount La Verna in 1224 and died in 1226 at age 44.

question: Around 1387 the English royal official Geoffrey Chaucer began a long poem framed as a story-telling contest among pilgrims travelling from London to Canterbury. He died in 1400 with the work unfinished. What is its name?
choices: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
context: Written in Middle English in a tradition that shaped the prestige of the vernacular. Chaucer was buried in Westminster Abbey, the first 'Poet's Corner.'

question: On 25 March 1436 Pope Eugene IV consecrated the new cathedral of Florence, crowned by a 45-meter dome built without external supports. The architect had studied Roman ruins and invented hoists and scaffolds for the job. Who was he?
context: It remains the largest brick dome ever built. Brunelleschi reportedly won the commission by challenging rivals to balance an egg on a marble slab.

question: In 1511 a Dutch humanist priest published a Latin satire dictated in a single week at the home of Thomas More in London. The book mocked church corruption from the mouth of personified Folly. Who wrote it?
context: Erasmus produced the first printed Greek New Testament in 1516, fueling Luther's challenge. He refused to break with Rome.

question: Beginning the night of 23-24 August 1572, in Paris, royal guards and Catholic mobs slaughtered the Huguenot leadership that had gathered for a wedding. The killings spread across France for weeks. What is the massacre called?
context: Estimates of dead range from 5,000 to 30,000. Henry of Navarre, the Protestant groom, survived by professing Catholicism and would later be king.

question: On 8 February 1587 at Fotheringhay Castle, after 19 years of imprisonment, a Catholic queen knelt at the block on the orders of her Protestant cousin Elizabeth I of England. She had been implicated in plots against the throne. Who was she?
context: The execution provoked outrage across Catholic Europe and contributed to the Spanish Armada the following year.

question: On 27 July 1656 the Jewish community of Amsterdam issued a cherem, or ban, against a 23-year-old member named Baruch Spinoza for 'abominable heresies.' He never recanted and ground lenses for a living. What did he later publish?
answer: The Ethics, an axiomatic system identifying God with nature
choices: The Ethics, an axiomatic system identifying God with nature
Meditations on First Philosophy in geometric order
Two Treatises of Government in defence of property
The City of God in answer to Augustine
context: Spinoza died of lung disease at 44 in 1677, likely worsened by glass dust. The Ethics was published months later.

question: In 1776, after 12 years of work, the Scottish professor of moral philosophy Adam Smith published a long treatise on the wealth of nations. He argued that self-interest channelled through free exchange enriched whole societies. What metaphor did he use?
answer: An invisible hand that guides private interest to public benefit
choices: An invisible hand that guides private interest to public benefit
A pilot light that ignites the engine of commerce
A blind watchmaker who fits each part to its place
A golden bridge that links labor to the king's treasury
context: Smith was a friend of David Hume and Edmund Burke. He saw commerce as a moral as well as material force, and warned against monopolies.

question: In 1705 the English astronomer Edmond Halley used Newton's laws and comet records of 1531, 1607, and 1682 to predict the return of one comet in 1758. It appeared on Christmas night 1758, after his death. What did it become?
answer: The first comet recognized as a periodic body, now bearing his name
choices: The first comet recognized as a periodic body, now bearing his name
Dimmed before perihelion and was lost to telescopes
Split into two pieces and confused the prediction
Returned six months late and discredited the theory
context: Halley funded the publication of Newton's Principia and catalogued southern stars from Saint Helena.

question: On 21 February 1804 a Cornish mining engineer ran the first steam-powered locomotive along an ironworks tramway in Merthyr Tydfil, Wales. It hauled 10 tons of iron and 70 men nearly 16 km. Who built it?
context: Trevithick's engine worked but was too heavy for the cast-iron rails of the day. He died poor; Stephenson's later 'Rocket' won the fame.

question: In 1856 an English engineer announced a process for turning pig iron into steel by blowing air through the molten metal, burning off carbon, in a tilting pear-shaped vessel. What was his name?
context: The process cut steel cost roughly tenfold and enabled the railway, skyscraper, and battleship age. American producers including Andrew Carnegie scaled it.

question: On 24 May 1844 the American painter and inventor Samuel Morse, in the chamber of the US Supreme Court in Washington DC, tapped out a message on a new electric telegraph line to Baltimore. What were the first four words sent?
context: The line ran 64 km between the two cities. Within a generation cables spanned oceans; news that once took weeks moved in minutes.

context: The Spartans died fighting, surrounded. Herodotus says they fought with daggers, then with hands and teeth. The stone monument at the pass read: 'Go tell the Spartans, stranger passing by, that here, obedient to their laws, we lie.'

question: In 399 BC, an Athenian jury of 501 convicted Socrates of corrupting the youth and impiety. Asked to name his own penalty, he proposed Athens should feed him at public expense as a benefactor. The jury voted death by a wider margin than conviction. What did Socrates do when friends arranged his escape?
answer: Refused — the Crito records why he owed obedience to Athens's laws
choices: Refused — the Crito records why he owed obedience to Athens's laws
Fled to Megara within hours and continued teaching there until death
Went to Sparta in disguise to embarrass Athens by surviving in its rival
Accepted, and lived in Thessaly under an assumed name with Plato's help
context: Socrates drank the hemlock in the company of friends. Plato's Phaedo records his last hours and his last words: 'Crito, we owe a cock to Asclepius. Pay it, and don't forget.'

question: In 333 BC, Alexander the Great arrived at the Phrygian city of Gordium. An ancient prophecy held that whoever untied the elaborate knot binding the cart of King Midas would rule Asia. Generations had failed; the knot had no visible ends. According to Plutarch's account, what did Alexander do?
answer: He cut the knot in half with his sword and declared the prophecy fulfilled
choices: He cut the knot in half with his sword and declared the prophecy fulfilled
He spent three days untying it patiently, following the priestly tradition
He had his engineers dismantle the cart and expose the knot from below
He skipped Gordium entirely and pressed east, mocking it as superstition
context: Within the year Alexander defeated Darius III at Issus, took Phoenicia and Egypt the next year, and crushed Persia at Gaugamela in 331 BC — the prophecy fulfilled to the letter.

question: Around 240 BC, the chief librarian of Alexandria heard that at noon on the summer solstice in Syene, the sun cast no shadow in a deep well. In Alexandria, 800 km north, a pillar at that moment cast a shadow at 7.2 degrees. From this he calculated Earth's circumference to within a few percent. Who was he?
answer: Eratosthenes of Cyrene, third librarian of Alexandria
choices: Eratosthenes of Cyrene, third librarian of Alexandria
Aristarchus of Samos, who proposed heliocentrism that century
Hipparchus of Nicaea, who later built the first star catalog
Posidonius of Apamea, the Stoic who repeated the calculation
context: Eratosthenes's figure was about 39,000-46,000 km depending on his stadion. The true equatorial circumference is 40,075 km. His library would be repeatedly damaged and finally lost over the following six centuries.

question: In 508 BC, an Athenian aristocrat broke up the old tribal blocs and reorganized the citizen body into ten artificial tribes mixed by geography, so each tribe contained men from the city, coast, and hills. The new Council of 500 was filled by lot from these tribes. Who was the reformer?
answer: Cleisthenes — founder of direct Athenian democracy
choices: Cleisthenes — founder of direct Athenian democracy
Solon — but his reforms came nearly a century earlier, around 594 BC
Pisistratus — but he was the tyrant whose sons Cleisthenes succeeded
Pericles — but he deepened the reforms decades later, not in 508 BC
context: Pericles deepened the reforms in the 450s BC by paying jurors and council members, so poor citizens could afford to serve. The system lasted until Macedonian conquest in 322 BC.

question: On the Greek island of Cos in the late fifth century BC, a physician laid the foundation of a medical tradition that treated disease as natural, prognosis as systematic, and patient care as a sworn ethical duty. The oath in his name bound the physician to do no harm. Who was he?
answer: Hippocrates of Cos, born around 460 BC
choices: Hippocrates of Cos, born around 460 BC
Galen of Pergamon, Roman-era codifier of Greek medicine
Asclepiades of Bithynia, Roman who rejected Hippocratic humors
Dioscorides, first-century AD author of Materia Medica
context: The Hippocratic corpus of about 60 works was probably written by several authors. The oath, in modernized form, is still taken by graduating medical students worldwide.

question: Around 300 BC, a Phoenician merchant who had lost his cargo in a shipwreck arrived in Athens and began teaching under a painted colonnade in the Agora. His school taught that virtue is the only good, that emotions follow from judgments, and that we should accept what is not in our control. What was the school called?
answer: Stoicism — named for the Stoa Poikile, the painted porch
choices: Stoicism — named for the Stoa Poikile, the painted porch
Cynicism — taught by Diogenes a generation earlier in Athens
Epicureanism — taught in Epicurus's Garden, a rival school
Skepticism — founded by Pyrrho after Alexander's eastern wars
context: Zeno of Citium founded the school around 301 BC. Cleanthes and Chrysippus succeeded him; Seneca, Epictetus, and Marcus Aurelius gave the school its Roman flowering five centuries later.

question: The Cynic philosopher Diogenes of Sinope lived in a wine jar in Athens, slept in public, and mocked Plato as 'a Socrates gone mad.' According to Diogenes Laertius he walked about Athens by daylight carrying a lit lantern. When asked what he was doing, he gave a one-line answer. What was it?
answer: He said: 'Looking for an honest man'
choices: He said: 'Looking for an honest man'
He said: 'Burning the books of the Sophists for warmth'
He said: 'Showing the gods how poorly Athens is lit'
He said: 'Reading Anaximander, who needs no daylight'
context: When Alexander the Great visited and offered to grant any wish, Diogenes asked him to step out of his sunlight. Alexander reportedly said: 'If I were not Alexander, I would wish to be Diogenes.'

question: Three wars between Rome and Carthage spanned 118 years (264-146 BC) and ended with Carthage's complete destruction, its citizens enslaved, its fields salted by legend. The elder Cato ended every Senate speech, regardless of topic, with the same phrase. What was it?
choices: 'Cave canem' — 'Beware the dog,' a Pompeian inscription
'Roma victrix' — 'Rome the victor,' a later coin legend
context: The Third Punic War (149-146 BC) ended with Scipio Aemilianus sacking Carthage. He reportedly wept while watching it burn, quoting Homer that one day Rome too would fall.

question: On January 10, 49 BC, the proconsul of Gaul led the single legion he had with him across a small river that marked the boundary between his province and Italy. To cross with arms was, by law, civil war. He reportedly hesitated on the bank, then quoted a line from the Greek playwright Menander. Who and what?
answer: Julius Caesar — 'Alea iacta est' — 'The die is cast'
choices: Julius Caesar — 'Alea iacta est' — 'The die is cast'
Pompey the Great — 'Sit pro ratione voluntas' — 'Let will stand for reason'
Sulla the Dictator — 'Imperium servabo' — 'I shall keep command'
Mark Antony — 'Cedant arma togae' — 'Let arms yield to the toga'
context: By March Caesar held Italy; by August he had broken Pompey at Pharsalus the next year. Pompey fled to Egypt and was murdered on landing by Ptolemy XIII's courtiers.

question: On the night of July 18-19, AD 64, a fire broke out near the Circus Maximus and burned for nine days, destroying ten of Rome's fourteen districts. Suetonius and Tacitus disagree on whether Nero played the lyre while it burned, but agree on what he did to deflect the rumor he had set it himself. What did Nero do?
answer: Blamed and persecuted Christians — the first imperial persecution
choices: Blamed and persecuted Christians — the first imperial persecution
Blamed the Druids and outlawed Druidic religion in the western provinces
Blamed Senate factions and forced Seneca, his old tutor, to commit suicide
Blamed Jewish residents, accelerating the conflict that erupted in AD 66
context: Tacitus records that Christians were crucified, torn apart by dogs, and burned as torches in Nero's gardens. Peter and Paul are traditionally martyred under Nero, around AD 64-67.

question: The greatest Latin historian after Livy lived under Domitian, Nerva, Trajan, and Hadrian. His Annals and Histories cover Tiberius to Domitian; his shorter Germania (AD 98) describes the tribes east of the Rhine. He wrote with deliberate moral compression — pithier and more bitter than Livy. Who was he?
answer: Tacitus — Publius Cornelius Tacitus, c. AD 56-c. 120
choices: Tacitus — Publius Cornelius Tacitus, c. AD 56-c. 120
Suetonius — author of the Lives of the Twelve Caesars, same period
Cassius Dio — wrote in Greek a century later under the Severans
Ammianus Marcellinus — the late-fourth-century continuator of Tacitus
context: Tacitus is one of the few non-Christian sources for the historical Jesus and the Neronian persecution, in Annals XV.44. His prose is the touchstone of Latin historical compression.

question: Roman engineers transformed the empire's cities with a building material that hardens underwater, made from volcanic ash, lime, and seawater. The Pantheon's 43-meter unreinforced dome, still the largest in the world, was poured from it 1,900 years ago. What was the material?
answer: Opus caementicium — Roman concrete using pozzolana volcanic ash
choices: Opus caementicium — Roman concrete using pozzolana volcanic ash
Opus reticulatum — a wall facing of small pyramidal stones
Opus testaceum — fired brick facing over a rubble core
Opus signinum — a waterproof mortar with crushed terracotta
context: Modern research has found that Roman concrete actually grows stronger in seawater because of chemical reactions with pozzolana. Many imperial structures stand today; their reinforced-steel modern counterparts will not.

question: Around AD 530, a hermit at a hilltop monastery south of Rome wrote a 73-chapter rule of life for monastic communities. It balanced prayer, manual labor, and study; it set hours, food, and clothing; it has shaped Western monasticism for 1,500 years. Who was the founder, and where?
answer: Benedict of Nursia — at Monte Cassino in central Italy
choices: Benedict of Nursia — at Monte Cassino in central Italy
Cassian — at Marseille, two generations earlier with a different rule
Columba — at Iona, but Celtic monasticism took a different form
Patrick — in Ireland, but his mission was diocesan, not monastic
context: Cassiodorus founded Vivarium nearby, copying classical texts. Together, the Benedictine network preserved much of the Latin literary inheritance through the centuries when Western cities collapsed.

question: In June 1633, a 69-year-old astronomer kneeling in penitential garb before the Roman Inquisition publicly abjured the doctrine that the earth moves. Sentenced to indefinite house arrest, he spent his remaining nine years at his villa near Florence going blind. What phrase does tradition say he muttered as he rose?
choices: 'Tempus fugit, veritas manet' — 'Time flies, truth remains'
'Roma locuta, causa finita' — 'Rome has spoken, the case is closed'
'Non possum non loqui' — 'I cannot but speak'
context: No contemporary source records the phrase. It first appears more than a century later. Pope John Paul II in 1992 acknowledged the Church's error in the Galileo case.

question: In 1856 an English inventor read a paper to the British Association at Cheltenham describing a process for converting pig iron to steel by blowing air through it in a tilting vessel — burning out carbon and impurities. The price of steel fell from about £40 a ton to £6 a ton within a few years. Who?
answer: Henry Bessemer — knighted in 1879 for the process
choices: Henry Bessemer — knighted in 1879 for the process
William Kelly — American who developed a similar process independently 1851
Robert Mushet — Bessemer's collaborator on spiegeleisen, not the originator
Carl Wilhelm Siemens — but his open-hearth process is later and different
context: Cheap steel made possible long railroads, the Brooklyn Bridge, modern shipbuilding, and the skyscrapers of late-19th-century Chicago and New York.

question: In December 1776, with Washington's army in retreat across New Jersey, an English-born pamphleteer wrote a series of essays meant to be read aloud to soldiers around campfires. The opening line is one of the most quoted in American letters. What is it?
answer: 'These are the times that try men's souls' — opening of The American Crisis
choices: 'These are the times that try men's souls' — opening of The American Crisis
'When in the course of human events' — opening of the Declaration, not Paine
'Government, even in its best state, is but a necessary evil' — Paine but earlier
'I know not what course others may take' — Patrick Henry in 1775, not Paine
context: Washington reportedly had the essay read aloud to his troops before the crossing of the Delaware. Paine wrote thirteen Crisis essays through the war, refusing any payment.

question: After the Boston Massacre of March 5, 1770, no Boston lawyer would defend the eight British soldiers facing murder charges. One young attorney took the case — believing every defendant deserved counsel — and won acquittal for six and reduced charges for the other two. Years later he called it among the most honorable acts of his life. Who?
answer: John Adams — second president, signing his career to legal principle
choices: John Adams — second president, signing his career to legal principle
John Hancock — but Hancock was the wealthy merchant client
James Otis — but Otis was the established radical, not the defender
Josiah Quincy II — Quincy co-counseled with Adams but did not lead the defense
context: Adams's defense rested on the legal claim that the soldiers had been provoked into reasonable fear of grievous harm. The verdict — manslaughter convictions reduced to thumb branding for two soldiers, acquittal for six — was widely accepted as a fair outcome.

question: In 1797, three French foreign ministry agents — labeled X, Y, and Z in the diplomatic correspondence sent to Congress — demanded a bribe and a loan to France before they would even meet with American envoys sent by President Adams. American public reaction was outrage. What phrase summed up the response?
answer: 'Millions for defense, but not one cent for tribute'
choices: 'Millions for defense, but not one cent for tribute'
'We will not be Britain's poodle nor France's spaniel'
'Give us the price of peace or we give you the cost of war'
'Neither vassals to France nor lapdogs to Britain'
context: The actual phrase is from a later toast attributed to South Carolina envoy Charles Cotesworth Pinckney. The XYZ Affair triggered the undeclared Quasi-War with France (1798-1800), the Alien and Sedition Acts, and the Federalist Party's collapse in the 1800 election.

question: On the night of October 16, 1859, the abolitionist John Brown and 21 followers seized the federal arsenal at Harpers Ferry, Virginia, planning to arm enslaved people for revolt. Within 36 hours US Marines under Colonel Robert E. Lee captured Brown. He was hanged on December 2, 1859. What did Brown say or do?
answer: He left a note: 'the crimes of this guilty land will never be purged away but with blood'
choices: He left a note: 'the crimes of this guilty land will never be purged away but with blood'
He recanted, accepting Christian penance from a Virginia chaplain before dying
He named federal collaborators in a final letter that ignited Southern fears
He fled west and was killed in a separate Missouri raid the next year
context: Northern abolitionists revered Brown as a martyr; Southerners saw a terrorist. The raid widened the sectional gulf in the decisive year before Lincoln's election.

question: In early May 1863, Lee outmaneuvered Joseph Hooker's much larger Union army in the Virginia Wilderness with a daring division of his own outnumbered force. Stonewall Jackson led 28,000 men around the Union right flank and crushed it. That night, returning to his lines, Jackson was shot by friendly fire. What happened?
answer: Jackson's left arm was amputated; he died of pneumonia eight days later
choices: Jackson's left arm was amputated; he died of pneumonia eight days later
Jackson recovered but was killed at Gettysburg two months later
Jackson was paralyzed but lived in Virginia until the war's end
Jackson's wound healed; he died of typhoid in 1865 just before surrender
context: Lee said of Jackson: 'He has lost his left arm, but I have lost my right.' The loss of Jackson is often called the single greatest individual loss to the Confederate war effort. Lee invaded Pennsylvania weeks later — without him.

question: On November 19, 1863, at the dedication of a Pennsylvania military cemetery, the principal speaker was Edward Everett, who spoke for two hours. The president followed with a 272-word address that took about two minutes. Newspapers at the time gave more attention to Everett. What is the line that opens the address?
answer: 'Four score and seven years ago' — referring to 1776
choices: 'Four score and seven years ago' — referring to 1776
'We are met on a great battlefield' — but that comes later in the address
'Fourscore and twelve years ago' — wrong arithmetic for 1776 from 1863
'Of the people, by the people, for the people' — but that closes it
context: Everett wrote Lincoln the next day: 'I should be glad if I could flatter myself that I came as near to the central idea of the occasion in two hours as you did in two minutes.' The speech is now considered the central statement of American democratic creed.

question: On March 9, 1864, Lincoln promoted a 41-year-old major general to lieutenant general — a rank previously held in full only by George Washington. He took command of all Union armies and established his headquarters in the field with the Army of the Potomac in Virginia. Who?
answer: Ulysses S. Grant — finally the general Lincoln had been seeking
choices: Ulysses S. Grant — finally the general Lincoln had been seeking
William Tecumseh Sherman — but Sherman commanded under Grant
Philip Sheridan — but Sheridan was a corps commander, not yet army
George Thomas — 'the Rock of Chickamauga,' but never lieutenant general
context: Grant's strategy was simultaneous pressure on all Confederate armies — denying Lee the ability to shift troops to threatened sectors. The war was over thirteen months later.

question: Just before 8 a.m. on Sunday, December 7, 1941, the Imperial Japanese Navy attacked the US Pacific Fleet's main base in Hawaii. Six Japanese carriers launched 353 aircraft in two waves; 2,403 Americans died; 19 ships were sunk or heavily damaged including the battleship Arizona. What did FDR call the next day in his speech to Congress?
answer: 'A date which will live in infamy'
choices: 'A date which will live in infamy'
'A treacherous and unparalleled act of war'
'A morning that will never be forgotten'
context: Congress declared war on Japan within one hour. Germany declared war on the United States December 11. The American carriers — the Lexington, Enterprise, and Saratoga — were at sea during the attack and would prove decisive in the Pacific war.

question: At 8:15 a.m. local time on August 6, 1945, a B-29 Superfortress named for the pilot's mother dropped a uranium-fueled atomic bomb on a Japanese city of 350,000. The bomb, code-named 'Little Boy,' produced an explosion equivalent to 15 kilotons of TNT. Roughly 70,000 died immediately, 140,000 by year's end. What city?
answer: Hiroshima — destroyed by the first wartime atomic bomb
choices: Hiroshima — destroyed by the first wartime atomic bomb
Nagasaki — but Nagasaki was the second target, on August 9
Tokyo — but Tokyo was firebombed conventionally in March 1945
Kokura — but Kokura was Nagasaki's original target, switched for weather
context: The pilot of the Enola Gay was Colonel Paul Tibbets. Japan did not surrender; the second bomb fell on Nagasaki three days later. Emperor Hirohito's radio broadcast accepting surrender came on August 15.

question: On December 1, 1955, a 42-year-old Black seamstress and NAACP secretary in Montgomery, Alabama, refused to give up her seat to a white passenger and was arrested. The Black community boycotted city buses for 381 days, led by a 26-year-old new pastor. Who were they?
answer: Rosa Parks (arrested) and Martin Luther King Jr. (led the boycott)
choices: Rosa Parks (arrested) and Martin Luther King Jr. (led the boycott)
Rosa Parks (arrested) and Ralph Abernathy (led the boycott)
Claudette Colvin (arrested) and Martin Luther King Jr. (led the boycott)
Mary Louise Smith (arrested) and E. D. Nixon (led the boycott)
context: King's leadership of the Montgomery Improvement Association launched his national career. Browder v. Gayle (1956) ended segregation on Montgomery's buses; the modern civil rights movement had its first major victory.

question: On July 20, 1969, at 20:17 UTC, the lunar module Eagle touched down on the Moon's Sea of Tranquility. Six hours later, the American mission commander stepped onto the surface and spoke a line slightly garbled by transmission. What does the transmitted recording say?
answer: 'That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind'
choices: 'That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind'
'Houston, the Eagle has landed, and the heavens are open'
'I have walked, and I have walked, and the moon is silent'
'For all mankind, this is a moment of peace'
context: Neil Armstrong said he had intended 'one small step for a man' — the indefinite article lost in static. Edwin 'Buzz' Aldrin joined him on the surface; Michael Collins remained in lunar orbit. Apollo 11 fulfilled Kennedy's 1961 pledge.

question: On June 12, 1987, before a crowd at the Brandenburg Gate in West Berlin — with the Wall directly behind him — President Reagan addressed the Soviet leader by name. State Department officials had repeatedly tried to remove the line from drafts. Reagan kept putting it back. What was the line?
choices: 'Mr. Gorbachev, dismantle this barrier of fear!'
'Mr. Gorbachev, let the Berliners go home!'
context: The Wall came down on November 9, 1989 — two years and five months later. Critics had derided the speech as empty bluster; historians have reassessed it as a moment that helped accelerate the collapse of Soviet power in Eastern Europe.

question: On the morning of September 11, 2001, 19 hijackers from al-Qaeda flew four passenger airliners. Two struck the World Trade Center in New York; both 110-story towers collapsed within two hours. A third struck the Pentagon. The fourth, United Flight 93, crashed in a Pennsylvania field after passengers fought back. How many people died total?
answer: Roughly 2,977 victims plus the 19 hijackers — the deadliest attack on US soil
choices: Roughly 2,977 victims plus the 19 hijackers — the deadliest attack on US soil
Roughly 1,500 victims, the lowest range of early estimates that morning
Roughly 4,500 victims, the highest range of early estimates
Roughly 6,000 victims plus the hijackers, an early erroneous figure
context: The attacks triggered the US wars in Afghanistan (October 2001) and Iraq (March 2003). They reshaped American politics, foreign policy, security architecture, and immigration policy for at least two decades.

question: Between 1950 and 1953, the new Chinese Communist regime imposed mass-mobilization land reform. Peasants were urged at struggle sessions to denounce, beat, and kill landlords. Estimates of those killed in the campaigns vary widely from rough Soviet-style figures to higher Chinese internal documents. What is the broadly accepted range?
answer: Roughly 2 to 5 million killed, with millions more sent to labor camps
choices: Roughly 2 to 5 million killed, with millions more sent to labor camps
Roughly 500,000 to 800,000 killed, comparable to Soviet figures
Roughly 10 to 15 million killed in the broader famine context
Roughly 100,000 to 200,000 killed in carefully limited targeted purges
context: The campaigns destroyed the rural landlord class as a social category. Land was redistributed to peasants — then taken back through collectivization a few years later, then again in the Great Leap Forward. The communist death toll under Mao continued to mount.

question: In 1956 Mao called for free criticism of party rule with the slogan 'Let a hundred flowers bloom, let a hundred schools of thought contend.' Surprised by the depth of resentment, he abruptly reversed in mid-1957 and launched an anti-rightist campaign. How many were purged?
answer: Roughly 500,000 — intellectuals, teachers, journalists, party members
choices: Roughly 500,000 — intellectuals, teachers, journalists, party members
Roughly 50,000 — a smaller, contained anti-Khrushchevite faction
Roughly 5 million — including peasants who had spoken at struggle meetings
Roughly 5,000 — only the most prominent intellectuals were affected
context: Whether Mao always intended the campaign as a trap or genuinely changed his mind remains historically disputed. Either way, the Hundred Flowers/Anti-Rightist sequence broke any remaining willingness among Chinese intellectuals to speak honestly about the regime.

question: On June 5, 1989, the day after Chinese troops cleared Tiananmen Square, an unidentified man in a white shirt carrying shopping bags stepped in front of a column of Type 59 tanks on Chang'an Avenue near the Beijing Hotel. He refused to move; the lead tank tried to drive around him; he stepped back into its path. Several Western photographers captured the scene. What is the man called?
answer: 'Tank Man' — his identity has never been confirmed
choices: 'Tank Man' — his identity has never been confirmed
Wang Weilin — a name later popularized but never confirmed
Zhao Ziyang — but that was the deposed general secretary, separate figure
Wuer Kaixi — but that was the student leader, who escaped to Taiwan
context: Whether Tank Man survived is unknown. The image is one of the most reproduced of the 20th century. It remains censored within China; foreign websites carrying it are blocked.

question: On September 10, 1989, the reform communist government of Hungary opened its border with Austria. Within weeks, tens of thousands of East Germans on summer vacation in Hungary streamed across into the West. The exodus undermined the entire East German state. What was the border called?
answer: The Iron Curtain — its first major breach since 1948
choices: The Iron Curtain — its first major breach since 1948
The Inner German Border — but that was the East-West German line directly
The Berlin Wall — but the Wall was a different specific border
The Carpathian Curtain — but no such phrase was historically used
context: Erich Honecker had ruled East Germany since 1971; he was deposed in October 1989. The Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989 — partly because hundreds of thousands of East Germans had already left through Hungary, Czechoslovakia, and Poland.

question: From roughly 2680 to 2180 BC, the Old Kingdom of Egypt — under the Third through Sixth Dynasties — built the great pyramids of the Giza necropolis. The Great Pyramid of Khufu (Cheops), the largest, stands 481 feet tall and contains 2.3 million stone blocks. What pharaoh built it?
answer: Khufu — Cheops in Greek, ruled c. 2589-2566 BC
choices: Khufu — Cheops in Greek, ruled c. 2589-2566 BC
Djoser — but Djoser built the earlier Step Pyramid at Saqqara
Khafre — but Khafre built the second pyramid at Giza, slightly smaller
Sneferu — but Sneferu built the Bent and Red Pyramids at Dahshur
context: The Great Pyramid was the tallest manmade structure in the world for nearly 4,000 years, until the spire of Lincoln Cathedral was built around 1311. Modern construction estimates suggest 20-30 years of work by perhaps 20,000 organized laborers.

question: Around 1200 AD, Polynesian settlers reached one of the most remote inhabited places in the world — a 64-square-mile volcanic island 2,300 miles west of South America and 1,300 miles southeast of Pitcairn. They carved nearly 900 stone heads (moai), the largest 33 feet tall, before the population crashed in the 17th-18th centuries. What is the local name?
answer: Rapa Nui — known to Europeans as Easter Island
choices: Rapa Nui — known to Europeans as Easter Island
Pitcairn — but Pitcairn is a separate, much smaller island
Aotearoa — but Aotearoa is the Maori name for New Zealand
Marquesas — but the Marquesas are a different Polynesian group
context: Jared Diamond's 'Collapse' (2005) made Easter Island a parable of environmental destruction. More recent research suggests rat infestation (brought by the settlers) and European-introduced disease, not deforestation alone, drove the demographic crash.

question: On June 7, 1954, a 41-year-old British mathematician was found dead in his bed at his home in Wilmslow, near Manchester. Half a cyanide-laced apple lay beside him. The verdict at inquest was suicide, although his mother and others have argued it may have been an accident. Who?
answer: Alan Turing — pioneer of computer science, dead at 41
choices: Alan Turing — pioneer of computer science, dead at 41
John von Neumann — but von Neumann died of cancer in 1957, three years later
Kurt Gödel — but Gödel starved himself to death in 1978, much later
Ludwig Wittgenstein — but Wittgenstein died of cancer in 1951
context: Turing had been chemically castrated by a 1952 court order after being convicted of 'gross indecency' for a homosexual relationship. He was granted a royal pardon in 2013, and the 'Alan Turing Law' in 2017 extended pardon to others convicted under the same statute.

question: Visiting Ramanujan in a Putney sanatorium in 1919, G. H. Hardy mentioned that he had arrived in a taxi numbered 1729 — a rather dull number, he thought. Ramanujan immediately replied that it was actually quite interesting: the smallest number expressible as a sum of two cubes in two different ways. What are the two cube sums?
context: 1729 has been called the 'Hardy-Ramanujan number' or 'taxicab(2)' ever since. Ramanujan had a months-to-live spirit even on his deathbed; he died in April 1920 at 32. His name has entered mathematical folklore.

question: In 1909, working with Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden at Manchester, a New Zealand-born physicist directed a beam of alpha particles at a thin gold foil. Most went through; a few bounced almost straight back. He compared the result to firing a shell at tissue paper and having it ricochet. What did the result imply?
answer: Atoms contain a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus
choices: Atoms contain a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus
Atoms are a uniform 'plum pudding' of charge throughout their volume
Atoms exchange particles freely with their neighbors in a continuous medium
Atoms are mathematical abstractions with no spatial structure at all
context: Rutherford's gold-foil experiment overthrew J.J. Thomson's 'plum pudding' model. Niels Bohr's 1913 paper extended the picture with quantized electron orbits. Rutherford himself won the 1908 Nobel — for earlier work on radioactivity, not for the gold-foil discovery.

question: On the morning of December 17, 1903, on the windy dunes of the Outer Banks of North Carolina, two Ohio bicycle mechanics took turns making four powered flights in a 605-pound biplane. The first flight covered 120 feet in 12 seconds; the fourth and longest covered 852 feet in 59 seconds. Who took the first flight?
choices: Wilbur Wright — but Wilbur flew the longest flight, the fourth
Charlie Taylor — but Taylor was their mechanic, did not fly
John T. Daniels — but Daniels took the photograph, did not fly
context: Five spectators witnessed the flights; the photographer John T. Daniels captured the takeoff of Flight 1 — among the most reproduced photographs in history. The Wright brothers' patent claims dominated US aviation litigation for the next decade.

question: On the afternoon of February 22, 1980, at the Lake Placid Olympics, an American hockey team of college players coached by Herb Brooks defeated the Soviet national team — heavily favored as four-time defending champions — 4 to 3. Mike Eruzione scored the winner. Al Michaels's call on ABC?
choices: 'Have you ever seen anything like it?'
context: The US team went on to beat Finland for the gold medal two days later. The game took place against the backdrop of the Iranian hostage crisis and Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, and was widely interpreted as a Cold War moral victory.

question: Just after 9 a.m. on Monday, August 18, 1969, the last performer to take the stage at the muddy three-day music festival on Max Yasgur's farm in upstate New York played a 3-minute, 43-second instrumental electric-guitar rendition of the American national anthem. Most of the original 400,000 attendees had already left. Who?
answer: Jimi Hendrix — performance now considered iconic
choices: Jimi Hendrix — performance now considered iconic
Janis Joplin — but Joplin had played the previous afternoon
Jefferson Airplane — but they played earlier in the festival
Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young — but they played late on day three
context: Hendrix's anthem rendition is widely regarded as a complex Vietnam-era political-musical statement. He died at 27 of barbiturate-induced asphyxia in London just over a year later, on September 18, 1970.

question: From 1958 to 1962, Mao's Great Leap Forward set absurdly high grain quotas based on falsified provincial reports. Officials confiscated grain regardless of local conditions to meet quotas. Peasants starved while granaries held seed grain. Local officials who reported the truth were purged. What was the death toll?
answer: Roughly 30 to 45 million deaths, mostly from starvation
choices: Roughly 30 to 45 million deaths, mostly from starvation
Roughly 5 to 10 million deaths, mostly in remote western provinces
Roughly 1 to 3 million deaths, mostly in the Anhui-Henan border region
Roughly 100 to 200 million deaths, the highest of any historical event
context: Frank Dikötter's Mao's Great Famine (2010), based on Chinese provincial archives, settled the conventional figure near 45 million. The Great Leap is the largest peacetime atrocity in human history. The Chinese state still strictly limits research and discussion.

question: In 399 BC, three Athenians — Meletus, Anytus, and Lycon — brought charges against Socrates for impiety and corrupting the youth. Tried before 501 citizen jurors, Socrates was convicted by a narrow margin. Plato's *Apology* records his defense; he refused to propose exile as an alternative. Crito offered to bribe the guards. What did Socrates do?
answer: He drank the prescribed hemlock, talking with his friends until his legs went numb
choices: He drank the prescribed hemlock, talking with his friends until his legs went numb
He fled by sea to Megara and continued teaching there until his death of fever
He retracted his teachings before the jury and was released under a permanent silence vow
He accepted exile to Thessaly and lived another decade under the protection of a local tyrant
context: Plato's *Phaedo* describes the death scene. Socrates told the jailer 'Crito, we owe a cock to Asclepius — pay it and do not neglect it' — possibly thanking the god of healing for his release from life. He left no written work; everything we have comes through Plato and Xenophon.

question: In 333 BC, the 23-year-old Alexander of Macedon arrived at the Phrygian capital of Gordium during his eastern campaign. Local tradition held that an intricate knot tied to a wagon could be undone only by the man destined to rule Asia. Alexander stepped up to it. What did he do?
answer: Cut the knot with one stroke of his sword rather than untangle it
choices: Cut the knot with one stroke of his sword rather than untangle it
Studied the rope for a day and unwound it carefully strand by strand
Refused the test, calling such prophecies unworthy of Macedonian arms
Burned the wagon, declaring the omen invalid by destruction
context: Plutarch's *Life of Alexander* gives the sword version; Aristobulus, a member of Alexander's staff, said he simply pulled the linchpin out of the yoke. Either way, the Phrygians took it as proof. He went on to defeat Darius III at Issus (333) and Gaugamela (331), and reached the Indus by 326 before his army refused to go farther.

question: Around 240 BC, Eratosthenes was head librarian at the Library of Alexandria. He knew that at noon on the summer solstice in Syene (modern Aswan), the sun shone straight down a deep well — no shadow. On the same day in Alexandria, vertical objects cast a shadow at an angle he measured as 1/50 of a circle. Combined with the road distance between the cities, what did he calculate?
answer: Earth's circumference at about 250,000 stadia — within roughly 1 percent of the true 40,000 km
choices: Earth's circumference at about 250,000 stadia — within roughly 1 percent of the true 40,000 km
Earth's diameter at about 8,000 stadia — used by Aristarchus to estimate the moon's distance
The sun's diameter at about 700,000 stadia — assuming the sun lay at infinite distance
The axial tilt at exactly 23 degrees — the figure Hipparchus refined a century later
context: Eratosthenes' result depended on the cities lying on the same meridian (close enough) and the sun being effectively at infinity (true). The stadion length is uncertain, but most reconstructions give him an error of 1–15 percent. The Greeks knew Earth was a sphere; Christopher Columbus used a smaller estimate from Ptolemy that helped convince his backers the Atlantic crossing was short.

question: On St. Crispin's Day, October 25, 1415, Henry V of England with about 6,000 troops (mostly longbowmen, the rest dysentery-afflicted men-at-arms) was caught by a French army at least three times its size on a muddy field in northern France. Henry placed his archers behind sharpened stakes. French knights, on foot in the mud, struggled forward through arrow showers. Many drowned in their armor in the marsh. What was the casualty ratio?
answer: Perhaps 6,000 French dead (including much of the nobility) against about 400 English
choices: Perhaps 6,000 French dead (including much of the nobility) against about 400 English
Perhaps 1,000 French dead against 300 English in roughly proportionate fighting
Perhaps 3,000 French dead and 2,500 English wounded in a closely contested fight
Perhaps 500 French and 100 English casualties — much smaller than legend suggests
context: Henry's controversial order to kill French prisoners during the battle (because he feared a renewed French attack) added to the casualty figure. The English wounded had been ordered to fight on as best they could. Shakespeare's *Henry V* (c. 1599), with the St. Crispin's Day speech, shaped English national memory. Henry died of dysentery 1422; English military prospects in France collapsed after Joan of Arc's intervention at Orleans 1429.

question: In early 1913, a 25-year-old Indian clerk in Madras — who had failed his university examinations because he neglected non-mathematical subjects — sent a letter to the Cambridge mathematician G.H. Hardy. The letter contained about 120 theorems, many in pure number theory. Hardy and his collaborator J.E. Littlewood reportedly worked through the letter into the night. Some theorems were known; some were wrong; some Hardy could not even understand. What was Hardy's conclusion?
answer: The theorems must be true — 'because if they were not true, no one would have the imagination to invent them'
choices: The theorems must be true — 'because if they were not true, no one would have the imagination to invent them'
The letter was a hoax produced by Cambridge undergraduates to test Hardy
The author had clearly studied Cambridge syllabus material in detail
The work was promising but lacked the rigor needed for serious publication
context: Hardy arranged for Srinivasa Ramanujan (1887–1920) to come to Cambridge. He arrived April 1914. Over five years they collaborated on partitions, modular forms, and other deep number-theoretic results. Ramanujan, a strict vegetarian, suffered from poor health in wartime England. He returned to India 1919 and died of (probably) tuberculosis or hepatic amoebiasis 1920 at 32. The 'lost notebook' of his last year's work was rediscovered 1976 and is still being mined for new mathematics.

question: Around 1784, in a one-room schoolhouse in the small German town of Braunschweig, a 7-year-old boy in mathematics class was set by his teacher the task of summing the integers from 1 to 100 — a task expected to take perhaps an hour. The boy wrote the answer on his slate in seconds: 5,050. He had noticed that 1+100, 2+99, 3+98, etc. — fifty pairs each summing to 101 — gave 50 × 101 = 5,050. Who was he?
answer: Carl Friedrich Gauss — became one of the greatest mathematicians in history
choices: Carl Friedrich Gauss — became one of the greatest mathematicians in history
Leonhard Euler — but Euler was Swiss, lived 1707–83, and was already dead by 1784
Pierre-Simon Laplace — but Laplace was French and an adult by 1784
Joseph-Louis Lagrange — but Lagrange was Italian-French and an adult by 1784
context: Gauss (1777–1855) showed exceptional mathematical talent from childhood; the Duke of Braunschweig supported his education at the local *Collegium Carolinum* and then at Göttingen. His *Disquisitiones Arithmeticae* (1801, age 24) is a foundational text of number theory. He held the chair at Göttingen 1807 until his death; he discovered the asteroid Ceres' orbit (1801) and made fundamental contributions to astronomy, geodesy, and electromagnetism. He kept many results secret for years through perfectionism — losing priority on non-Euclidean geometry, the geometric interpretation of complex numbers, and other areas.

question: On July 20, 1969, at 10:56 p.m. EDT, 38 minutes after the lunar module *Eagle* had landed in the Sea of Tranquility, the 38-year-old commander climbed down the ladder and stepped onto the lunar surface. He spoke to about 600 million television viewers worldwide. Who was he?
answer: Neil Armstrong — first human to walk on the Moon; commander of Apollo 11
choices: Neil Armstrong — first human to walk on the Moon; commander of Apollo 11
Buzz Aldrin — second human to walk on the Moon; followed Armstrong by 19 minutes
Michael Collins — Apollo 11 command module pilot, remained in lunar orbit
Pete Conrad — Apollo 12 commander, fourth human on the Moon (November 1969)
context: Armstrong (1930–2012) said 'That's one small step for [a] man, one giant leap for mankind' — the 'a' is heard inconsistently in the recording. He insisted he had said it. The plaque on the lunar module's leg reads 'We came in peace for all mankind.' Five more Apollo missions landed on the Moon (12, 14, 15, 16, 17); Apollo 13 (April 1970) was an aborted mission with successful recovery. Armstrong was famously private after the mission; he resented being treated as a national resource.

question: On April 13, 1970, about 56 hours into the mission, an oxygen tank in the Apollo 13 service module exploded — crippling the spacecraft 200,000 miles from Earth. Commander Jim Lovell radioed Houston with what became one of the most famous understatements in history. What did he say?
answer: 'Houston, we've had a problem' — often misquoted as 'Houston, we have a problem'
choices: 'Houston, we've had a problem' — often misquoted as 'Houston, we have a problem'
'Houston, we've lost an engine' — but the problem was more serious than engine loss
'Houston, please advise' — but the actual call was more specific than that
'Houston, oxygen has been compromised' — but Lovell's call was less technical than this
context: The Apollo 13 mission failed to land on the moon but succeeded in returning all three astronauts (Lovell, Fred Haise, Jack Swigert) safely to Earth on April 17, 1970. The lunar module *Aquarius*, designed for two people on the lunar surface, served as a lifeboat for three for four days. Flight director Gene Kranz's 'failure is not an option' became iconic. The Ron Howard film *Apollo 13* (1995) with Tom Hanks dramatized the rescue. NASA called the mission a 'successful failure.'
